design_detail: Narrative, debate-style review with no methods section: no search strategy, databases, dates or eligibility criteria. Treats amphetamine and methamphetamine together as amphetamines; draws on 1968–1979 experimental administration studies, case reports, community and clinical samples, Japanese clinical series, family and genetic studies, animal work and treatment literature (108 references), and proposes a stress–vulnerability model (Figure 1). No tables and no quantitative synthesis.
can_establish: The authors' reading of the pre-2012 literature and their hypothesis that amphetamine-associated psychosis and primary psychosis are linked through individual vulnerability rather than being separate entities.
cannot_establish: How often amphetamine-associated psychosis occurs, how long it lasts, or how it differs from schizophrenia with any stated precision, because the evidence was not systematically identified or appraised, amphetamine and methamphetamine are pooled, and several statements rest on case series, guidelines, a book review, animal studies or schizophrenia literature; the proposed model is not tested.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The cited evidence mixes experimental administration studies in volunteers, case reports in children treated for ADHD, community and treatment samples of people who use amphetamines, psychiatric admissions, Japanese clinical series of persistent and recurrent psychosis, family and genetic studies, and animal studies.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not reported: no search strategy, sources, dates or eligibility criteria are described.
sample.selection_effects: How sources were chosen is unstated and cannot be audited. Two cited primary studies on symptoms and drug use in methamphetamine-positive psychiatric admissions (refs 41 and 51, Medhus et al., 2012) come from the authors' own group. Some clinical statements rest on non-primary sources: faster recovery is cited to a 1958 monograph, a 1959 book review, a 2006 management guideline and one 6-month follow-up study (refs 60–63).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The authors note that reported psychosis rates depend on whether self-report or formal diagnostic instruments were used (Prevalence and clinical presentation, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Only as study conditions of the cited experiments: amphetamine was given in increasing doses until psychosis appeared, often after a total of 100–300 mg, and symptoms subsided within 6 days (refs 20–23). The authors state it is poorly understood whether psychosis at the end of a binge depends on the amount used, binge length, sleep deprivation or the user's vulnerability (Prevalence and clinical presentation, 1st–2nd paragraphs).
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed only qualitatively: people often end binges with alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids or cannabis, and use of these drugs is listed among possible risk factors for psychosis (Prevalence and clinical presentation, 2nd paragraph; Risk factors, 2nd paragraph).

comparison.controls: Not applicable. Comparisons with schizophrenia are drawn from cited studies whose designs and sizes are not given.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The paper's central argument is that premorbid vulnerability (schizophrenia, schizotypal traits, family history, prodromal cognitive dysfunction, earlier amphetamine psychosis) decides who becomes psychotic, but it cites no study that measured vulnerability before amphetamine exposure.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable; no instruments are specified.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed beyond the contrast between self-report and formal diagnostic instruments.
outcomes.operationalization: Psychosis, acute versus chronic psychosis and primary psychosis are used in their clinical senses without diagnostic criteria, instruments or thresholds. Amphetamine and methamphetamine are not separated.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The quantitative statements are all second-hand: psychosis reported in 8–46% of regular users of amphetamines; experimental psychosis often after 100–300 mg in total with resolution within 6 days; relatives of methamphetamine users with a lifetime psychosis 5 times more likely to have schizophrenia; up to 25% of people first diagnosed with drug-induced psychosis developing a primary psychotic disorder after some years, more for methamphetamine; a 2008 review finding 18 papers on substance-induced psychosis, 7 on stimulants, one with a 1-year follow-up; one randomized trial (olanzapine vs haloperidol) in a 2009 Cochrane review.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed because no search or selection is described. Evidence that cuts against the vulnerability model is acknowledged only in passing (not all volunteers in the early experiments became psychotic).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A narrative synthesis of mixed and mostly indirect evidence: psychosis is common among regular users of amphetamines (8–46% in cited studies, varying with population, sex, pattern of use and instrument); acute symptoms overlap with acute schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis; several vulnerability factors and shared susceptibility genes are reported; long-term course is poorly studied (one stimulant study with a 1-year follow-up in the review the authors cite).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says amphetamine-induced psychosis seems to recover faster and appears to resolve more completely than schizophrenic psychosis. The body supports faster recovery with a 1958 monograph, a 1959 book review, a 2006 management guideline and one 6-month follow-up (refs 60–63), says in the same paragraph that recovery may be incomplete and that Japanese series describe psychosis lasting years, and later cites up to 25% of drug-induced psychoses becoming primary psychotic disorders. The abstract's statement that shared genes probably lower the threshold for psychosis and worsen its course is cited to a review and a book chapter (refs 32, 58). The stress–vulnerability model and the clinical advice drawn from it (closer monitoring for chronic development, strongly discouraging further use, research on preventive treatment) are hypotheses not tested in the paper.

timeline.event: This narrative review proposes a stress–vulnerability model linking amphetamine-associated and primary psychosis

Callaghan et al. (American Journal of Psychiatry) California record-linkage cohort on methamphetamine use and later schizophrenia, cited here as newly published support for a cannabis-like association

Wearne & Cornish narrative review of direct comparisons: persistent methamphetamine psychosis resembled schizophrenia on positive symptoms and cognition, schizophrenia had more negative symptoms; cites this paper

replication.where_it_stands: The vulnerability–stress account remains a hypothesis. Later direct comparisons, as summarized by Wearne & Cornish (2018), found persistent methamphetamine psychosis hard to separate from schizophrenia on positive symptoms and cognition, which is consistent with, but does not demonstrate, shared vulnerability.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: None of the authors declared conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Norwegian Centre for Addiction Research (SERAF), University of Oslo; Department of Clinical Neuroscience, Karolinska Institutet; Department of Biological and Medical Psychology, University of Bergen. The first author's group produced two of the cited primary studies (refs 41 and 51). Received 29 February 2012, accepted 11 September 2012.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people who use methamphetamine with vulnerability measured early (family history, schizotypy, prodromal symptoms, cognition, polygenic risk), repeated toxicology-verified exposure data and structured psychosis assessments, followed long enough to observe first episodes, recovery and transition to primary psychotic disorder; the model predicts that the exposure preceding a first episode is lower in people with higher measured vulnerability.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is a debate-style narrative review that does not claim to be systematic; AMSTAR 2 is applied for consistency with the encyclopedia's other review cards and fails all five applicable critical items. Items 11, 12 and 15 do not apply (no meta-analysis). The paper is usable as a statement of the vulnerability hypothesis and as a pointer to primary studies, not as evidence for frequency, duration or differential features of methamphetamine psychosis.

key_findings.finding: Psychosis is reported in 8–46% of regular users of amphetamines across the cited studies (refs 31–37); the authors attribute the spread to the population studied, sex, method and duration of use, and whether psychosis was assessed by self-report or formal diagnostic instruments.
key_findings.note: Amphetamine and methamphetamine are pooled; the range cannot be attributed to methamphetamine alone.

key_findings.finding: Cited experiments (refs 20–23) gave amphetamine in increasing doses until psychosis appeared, often after 100–300 mg in total; symptoms subsided within 6 days, antipsychotics blocked the effect, and not all participants became psychotic, some being withdrawn because of raised heart rate, blood pressure or temperature.
key_findings.note: Study conditions of 1968–1979 experiments, reported second-hand.

key_findings.finding: Only a weak relation between blood amphetamine level and psychotic symptoms has been reported in psychotic patients (refs 51, 52); the authors read this as pointing either to poor measurement of cumulative exposure or to individual vulnerability as the main risk factor.

Acute symptoms resemble acute schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis (persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, disorganized thinking, lack of insight); some studies report more grandiosity and visual hallucinations and less formal thought disorder in amphetamine psychosis, but the authors judge separation on acute symptoms probably very difficult.

Course: amphetamine psychosis is said to recover faster than schizophrenic psychosis (refs 60–63) and to resolve with abstinence, though possibly incompletely (ref 43); Japanese clinical series describe psychosis lasting up to several years and stress-triggered spontaneous relapses after remission, with family history of psychosis among the vulnerability factors.
key_findings.note: Refs 60–63 are a 1958 monograph, a 1959 book review, a 2006 guideline and a 6-month follow-up study.

key_findings.finding: Risk factors listed: previous amphetamine psychosis (sensitization), schizophrenia, schizotypal traits, amphetamine use disorder, other psychiatric disorders (attenuated psychosis, personality and affective disorders), early cognitive dysfunction, family history of mental disorder, and use of opioids, benzodiazepines, cannabis or alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, 1st–2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: A list of reported associations without effect sizes.

key_findings.finding: Relatives of methamphetamine users with a lifetime amphetamine psychosis are reported as 5 times more likely to have schizophrenia (ref 85); people with schizophrenia and with amphetamine psychosis both show higher plasma norepinephrine than non-psychotic methamphetamine users and non-users (refs 65, 88).
key_findings.locator: Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The sentence compares relatives of users with psychosis to users without psychosis; the intended comparison group is presumably their relatives. Check ref 85.

key_findings.finding: Treatment: a 2009 Cochrane review found one eligible randomized trial, in which olanzapine and haloperidol were both effective for amphetamine psychosis; the authors raise, from indirect evidence, a concern that dopamine D2 blockade may increase anhedonia and relapse, and mention benzodiazepines as an alternative.
key_findings.locator: Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Up to 25% of people first diagnosed with drug-induced psychosis develop a primary psychotic disorder after some years (ref 100), with higher figures for methamphetamine-induced psychosis (ref 67); a 2008 review found 18 papers on the clinical characteristics or outcomes of substance-induced psychosis, 7 on stimulants and only 1 with a 1-year follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Proposed model: amphetamine exposure acts as a stressor whose effect depends on vulnerability (less vulnerable people need more exposure to become psychotic), and repeated use may itself raise vulnerability through sensitization, so amphetamine-associated and primary psychosis are treated as linked phenomena rather than separate entities.
key_findings.locator: A model for the relationship…, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Clinical implications proposed from the model, not tested: closer monitoring of people diagnosed with amphetamine-induced psychosis for chronic development, strong discouragement of further use, and research on preventive psychosocial, psychoeducational and pharmacological interventions.
key_findings.locator: A model for the relationship…, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Amphetamine and methamphetamine are pooled under one term throughout, while some cited findings concern methamphetamine only.
reporting_issues.consequence: No figure in this paper can be attributed to methamphetamine specifically without checking the cited source.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says amphetamine psychosis appears to resolve more completely than schizophrenic psychosis; the body says recovery may be incomplete, cites Japanese series of psychosis lasting years, and cites up to 25% later transition to primary psychosis.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract overstates the completeness of recovery relative to the paper's own body text.

reporting_issues.issue: Several citations do not match their claims by title: faster recovery cites a monograph, a book review and a guideline (refs 60–62); treatability of amphetamine psychosis with antipsychotics cites a meta-analysis of antipsychotics in schizophrenia (ref 90); a sentence on Japanese research cites a US case report (ref 64); the community-availability correlation (refs 41–44) includes papers whose titles concern symptom comparison in admissions and sensitization (refs 41, 43); human sensitization to psychosis cites a cocaine study (ref 73).
reporting_issues.consequence: Each statement must be traced to an appropriate primary source before the encyclopedia uses it.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 is an image; only its legend was read as text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The model diagram was appraised from the legend and the surrounding text.
